recent_posts.title: Callgraph analysis
recent_posts.summary: Ferrous Systems explores multiple approaches to statically verifying that certain functions are never called in a Rust program, motivated by Ferrocene's need to certify a subset of `core` to IEC 61508 (SIL-2). Approaches covered include Clippy lints, effect type systems, linker-based tricks (no-panic), cfg hacks, and ultimately a custom rustc compiler driver. The chosen solution implements a callgraph analysis with two passes: a pre-monomorphization THIR pass for fast `cargo check` feedback, and a post-monomorphization MIR pass for reliable certification-grade analysis. The tool catches panics, unvalidated function calls, function pointer coercions, and dynamic trait object casts, even across crate boundaries and through generics.

recent_posts.title: Accessing Hardware in Rust
recent_posts.summary: A deep dive into hardware access patterns in Rust for bare-metal embedded systems. Covers three hardware access mechanisms: I/O ports, system/co-processor registers, and memory-mapped I/O (MMIO). Explains why volatile writes are required for MMIO, why creating Rust references to MMIO addresses is unsound, and how bitfields within registers are typically handled. Compares four major Rust MMIO abstraction crates — svd2rust, tock-registers, safe-mmio, and derive-mmio — evaluating each on API ergonomics, documentation discoverability, soundness, and AArch64 hypervisor compatibility. Also highlights the importance of running cargo doc to validate the developer experience of generated documentation.

recent_posts.title: Ferrocene for Air-Gapped Environments
recent_posts.summary: Ferrous Systems is developing an air-gapped environment feature for Ferrocene, its safety-qualified Rust compiler toolchain. The feature allows organizations to use Ferrocene and vetted Rust crates in isolated, internet-disconnected environments. A transfer zone with internet access handles central downloads; once inside the air-gapped environment, files are served via a local server and offline crates instance. The feature offers full control over which toolchain versions and packages are permitted, supports compliance workflows, and is planned for the 26.08 Ferrocene release. A demo is being shown at embedded world 2026.

recent_posts.title: Student Assistant
recent_posts.summary: Ferrous Systems is hiring a student assistant to work on rust-analyzer, the Language Server Protocol implementation for Rust. The role involves fixing bugs, adding features, triaging issues, and creating pull requests. Requirements include enrollment at a German university, fundamental Rust knowledge, and strong organizational skills. The position offers 15-20 hours per week at €20/hour, fully remote within Germany, with a focus on open-source contribution.

recent_posts.title: Research Engineer
recent_posts.summary: Ferrous Systems seeks a Research Engineer for a 3-year project focused on formal modeling, implementation, and verification of a Rust subset, plus network protocol assurance. The role involves contributing to Rust's formal semantics, implementing and proving portions of a network stack in Rust/Rocq, and publishing academic papers. Candidates need a master's in CS, formal verification experience (particularly with Rocq ITP), Rust knowledge, and ideally understanding of Rust semantics including unsafe code. The position offers PhD pursuit opportunities with academic partners, remote work in Germany, 35-40 hours/week, and potential permanent employment after the project period.

recent_posts.title: Ferrous Systems Achieves IEC 61508 (SIL 2) Certification for Rust Core Library Subset
recent_posts.summary: Ferrous Systems has achieved TÜV SÜD certification for a subset of Rust's core library according to IEC 61508 (SIL 2) standards, included in their Ferrocene 25.11.0 toolchain. This certification removes a major barrier for using Rust in safety-critical and embedded systems across regulated industries like automotive, medical devices, and industrial automation. The core library subset is essential for no_std applications and embedded development. Companies including Sonair and Kiteshield are already integrating the certified toolchain into safety-critical products, with Ferrocene supporting multiple safety standards including ISO 26262 (ASIL D) and IEC 61508 (SIL 3).

recent_posts.title: Ferrocene 25.11.0 now available!
recent_posts.summary: Ferrocene 25.11.0 is now available, featuring the first IEC 61508 (SIL 2) certified subset of Rust's core library. This qualified Rust toolchain enables developers to build certifiable code for safety-critical industrial systems across multiple architectures. The release includes changes from Rust 1.89 and 1.90, supports qualification for ISO 26262 (ASIL D), IEC 61508 (SIL 3), and IEC 62304 (Class C), and is 100% compatible with the main Rust compiler. The certified core subset provides access to essential Rust types like Option, Clone, str, and primitives, making it easier to develop high-assurance software without massive upfront investment.

recent_posts.title: Ferrocene 25.08.0 now available!
recent_posts.summary: Ferrocene 25.08.0 is now available, bringing a qualified Rust toolchain for safety-critical systems with ISO 26262, IEC 61508, and IEC 62304 certifications. This release includes compiler updates from Rust 1.87 and 1.88, featuring new APIs, safe architecture intrinsics, and naked functions. The team is also working on certifying a subset of the core library to IEC 61508 (SIL 2), planned for release in 25.11.0. Ferrocene is available for €25/month per user and supports x86_64 Linux, QNX Neutrino, and various RTOS platforms on Armv8-A and Armv7E-M architectures.

recent_posts.title: Rust: Who, What and Why for ESA SW PA Workshop
recent_posts.summary: Comprehensive overview of Rust adoption across industries, from cloud hyperscalers like Google and AWS to safety-critical applications in automotive, aerospace, and medical devices. Covers production deployments in Microsoft Windows kernel components, Samsung SmartThings, and Volvo vehicles, plus academic research for space applications including ESA OPS-SAT missions. Details qualified toolchains like Ferrocene for safety certification and emerging Rust-based operating systems.

recent_posts.title: Ferrous Systems Joins SOAFEE Initiative
recent_posts.summary: Ferrous Systems has joined the SOAFEE initiative to bring Rust programming language expertise to software-defined vehicles and embedded edge systems. The company contributes Rust safety and performance capabilities through their Ferrocene qualified compiler toolchain, supporting SOAFEE's mission to create open, cloud-native software standards for the automotive industry. Ferrous Systems will participate in working groups focused on safety, toolchains, runtime environments, and C/C++ integration.

top_posts.title: defmt is now 1.0
top_posts.summary: The defmt logging framework for embedded systems has reached version 1.0. This release ensures full compatibility with previous versions. Users can upgrade from defmt 0.3 to 1.0 by running 'cargo update'. The semver-trick has been used to make this transition smooth. Feedback on the new release is welcome via the issue tracker.

top_posts.title: Ferrocene 24.08.0 now available!
top_posts.summary: Ferrocene 24.08.0 has been released, bringing the latest Rust updates, increased target support, and a preview of the QNX toolchain for Rust. It is a fully open-source, safety-critical Rust compiler qualified to the highest safety levels (ASIL D and SIL 4). This version upgrades from Rust 1.76.0 to 1.79.0, includes experimental support for Windows and macOS, and offers cross-compilation for Armv7-R and Armv8-R. Ferrocene commits to quarterly releases and offers subscription plans for access.

top_posts.title: Ferrocene 25.05.0 now available!
top_posts.summary: Ferrocene 25.05.0 is now available, featuring the first Rust compiler toolchain qualified for safety-critical systems according to ISO 26262, IEC 61508, and IEC 62304 standards. This release includes upstream Rust improvements from versions 1.84-1.86 and adds qualified support for Armv7E-M bare-metal targets, enabling Rust development on ARM Cortex-M4/M7 processors in safety-critical contexts. Future releases will expand support to additional ARM targets including Cortex-A7, Cortex-R5F, and Cortex-M3/M33 processors.
